body.statement: For each \(\sigma\), let \(z_{\sigma}\) be the unique minimizer of \(f\) on nonempty \(H_{\sigma}\), with \(v_{\sigma}=f(z_{\sigma})\). The sector contains a legal model if and only if \(H_{\sigma}\ne\varnothing\), \(J_{\sigma}\) holds, and \[v_{\sigma}<M^2\quad\text{or}\quad\bigl(v_{\sigma}=M^2\ \text{and}\ 0<(z_{\sigma})_d<1\bigr).\] Moreover, for \(\omega\in\{-1,+1\}\), \(H_{(\omega,\omega)}\ne\varnothing\) if and only if \(-\omega t\max(s,u)\ge2\eta\Delta(s+u)\), and \(J_{(\omega,\omega)}\) holds if and only if the inequality is strict or \(s=u\) at equality; both opposite-sign sectors always satisfy \(J_{\sigma}\). Hence \(+1\in\mathcal P(\Sigma)\) exactly when one same-sign sector passes the certificate, and \(-1\in\mathcal P(\Sigma)\) exactly when one opposite-sign sector passes it.
body.justification: The theorem is the exact necessary-and-sufficient kernel and records open versus closed attainment instead of reporting an optimization infimum.
body.gap: vanSeeventerSalehkaleybar2026 gives an individual-edge zero criterion, while this theorem characterizes the joint product sign under simultaneous post-gauge magnitude and norm restrictions; trace one only selects the common time unit.
body.consumer: A bivariate graphical continuous Lyapunov analysis can report every loop polarity compatible with its covariance and declared scientific bounds.
body.proof_tex:
The certificate-completeness theorem gives the claimed norm and strict-attainment equivalence, so it remains to derive the scalar \(J_{\sigma}\) rules and connect sectors to polarity.  From the affine-fiber formula, with \(b=A_{12}\) and \(c=A_{21}\),
\[
 ub+sc
 =\frac{u(-dt/2-qs)+s(-(1-d)t/2+qu)}{\Delta}
 =-\frac{t\{s+(u-s)d\}}{2\Delta}. \tag{1}
\]
For the same-sign sector \((\omega,\omega)\), the two margin inequalities imply and, by the one-dimensional interval calculation below, are equivalent for fixed \(d\) to
\[
 -\omega t\{s+(u-s)d\}\ge 2\eta\Delta(s+u). \tag{2}
\]
Indeed the edge inequalities are bounds on \(q\):
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
b\ge\eta:&q\le(-\eta\Delta-dt/2)/s,\\
b\le-\eta:&q\ge(\eta\Delta-dt/2)/s,\\
c\ge\eta:&q\ge(\eta\Delta+(1-d)t/2)/u,\\
c\le-\eta:&q\le(-\eta\Delta+(1-d)t/2)/u.
\end{array} \tag{3}
\]
For equal signs, the relevant lower endpoint is no larger than the relevant upper endpoint exactly when (2) holds; equality permits their common endpoint.

The bracket \(s+(u-s)d\) is positive on \([0,1]\).  Since the right side of (2) is positive, feasibility forces \(-\omega t>0\).  The maximum of its left side over \(d\in[0,1]\) is
\[
 -\omega t\max(s,u).
\]
This proves
\[
 H_{(\omega,\omega)}\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 -\omega t\max(s,u)\ge2\eta\Delta(s+u). \tag{4}
\]
If (4) is strict, continuity permits a \(d\in(0,1)\) satisfying (2).  At equality, such an interior \(d\) exists precisely when the affine bracket is constant, namely when \(s=u\); if \(s\ne u\), its maximum occurs only at one endpoint.  This proves the stated rule for \(J_{(\omega,\omega)}\).

For \((\sigma_b,\sigma_c)=(+1,-1)\), (3) gives two upper bounds on \(q\); for \((-1,+1)\), it gives two lower bounds.  For any fixed \(d\in(0,1)\), choosing \(q\) below both upper bounds or above both lower bounds proves \(J_{\sigma}\).  Finally, both margins are strictly positive in magnitude, so their signs are exactly \((\sigma_b,\sigma_c)\).  Equal signs have product \(+1\), opposite signs have product \(-1\).  Taking the union of the legal sectors proves the two assertions about \(\mathcal P(\Sigma)\).
